title: The Gopis Perform the Katyayani Vow
story:
It was still dark when they left their houses. The young girls of Vrindavan went down to the river in the cold, before the first color of dawn touched the water, and slipped into the Yamuna while the stars were still out. This was not a game. It was a vow.

All through the first month of winter they rose while it was still night, every morning, and their mothers knew and said nothing. The river was cold, the air colder, and still they went. The winter had set its teeth into the cowherd land of Vraja; the ground was hard underfoot, and the water, when they entered it, took the breath away. But a vow begun in winter is not a thing to break because the morning is cold.

At the water's edge they made an image of the goddess Katyayani and worshipped it with everything they could bring — fragrant paste rubbed into the image, garlands hung about it, offerings laid before it, incense and a burning lamp held steady in the dark, so that the goddess they prayed to was never without light. And to her they spoke one prayer, the same prayer every day. "O Katyayani, great in power, great in mystery, sovereign of all," they said, "make Nanda's son my husband."

Nanda's son was Krishna, the cowherd boy of the village, who had grown up beside them; every girl who said the prayer knew exactly whom she meant.

That was the whole of it — one request, and no second list of wants. They did not ask for riches, or long life, or good fortune, the things a family might pray for on a daughter's behalf. They asked for him.

Rising at dawn, they went down to the water together, arms linked one with another, girl beside girl, so that the cold and the dark were shared between them. None of them went alone; none of them had to carry the whole weight of the vow by herself. There was something brave in the way they held one another against the morning.

Day after day the pattern held, and the month did not break it. What had begun as a private wish became a shared discipline, and the river saw the same small procession each dawn — the girls, the cold water, the lamp, the image, the one request. They did not waver and they did not grow tired; morning after morning they kept at it, the name of Nanda's son on their lips and the goddess before them. By the time the sun was fully up they were dressed and turning for home, and the day began as if nothing had happened — but the vow was one day nearer its end, and the river had one more morning of their prayer to keep.
reflection: The vow's force lies in what it leaves out. There is no petition for safety or prosperity, only the single, unhedged request — Nanda's son. And they ask together, arms linked, so that the longing itself becomes something shared rather than borne alone.
next_story_tease: But Krishna would soon find them at the river, and what he did there would test the vow they had made.
hero_scene: The young gopis standing in the cold water of the Yamuna before dawn, arms linked, worshipping an image of the goddess Katyayani by incense and lamplight as the first light touches the river.
